claim: During delayed ballistic reaches, motor areas consistently display movement-specific activity patterns prior to movement onset.
source: During delayed ballistic reaches, motor areas consistently display movement-specific activity patterns prior to movement onset.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Movement-specific activity patterns have been proposed to seed an initial neural state from which the movement unfolds.
source: while they have been proposed to seed an initial neural state from which the movement unfolds
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Recent experiments have uncovered the presence and necessity of ongoing inputs during movement.
source: recent experiments have uncovered the presence and necessity of ongoing inputs during movement
evidence: This refers to recent experimental findings, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Delay-period inputs consistently arise in an optimally controlled model of M1.
source: We find that delay-period inputs consistently arise in an optimally controlled model of M1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the modeling results presented in Figures 2-3.

claim: Optimal input-driven control of neural dynamics gives rise to multiple phases of preparation during reach sequences.
source: Finally, we show that optimal input-driven control of neural dynamics gives rise to multiple phases of preparation during reach sequences
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the modeling results in Figure 6.

claim: The motor cortex is thought to operate as a dynamical system whose state trajectories trace out the appropriate motor commands for downstream effectors.
source: During the production of ballistic movements, the motor cortex is thought to operate as a dynamical system whose state trajectories trace out the appropriate motor commands for downstream effectors (Shenoy et al., 2013; Miri et al., 2017; Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an established theoretical framework, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cortical state trajectories are empirically well described by a low-dimensional dynamical system evolving near-autonomously during movement.
source: First, cortical state trajectories are empirically well described by a low-dimensional dynamical system evolving near-autonomously during movement (Churchland et al., 2012; Pandarinath et al., 2018; Schimel et al., 2022)
evidence: This is presented as an empirical observation from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Movement-specific primary motor cortex (M1) activity arises well before movement initiation.
source: This input-driven seeding process is corroborated by observations of movement-specific primary motor cortex (M1) activity arising well before movement initiation (Lara et al., 2018; Kaufman et al., 2014; Churchland et al., 2012; Meirhaeghe et al., 2023; Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies and by Figure 1A showing neural data.

claim: The motor cortex receives critical pattern-generating input from the thalamus during movement production.
source: recent studies in mice have shown that the motor cortex receives critical pattern-generating input from the thalamus during movement production (Sauerbrei et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from recent experimental work, supported by citation.

claim: Most published network models of delayed reaches are able to perform the task just as well without preparatory inputs.
source: Moreover, most published network models of delayed reaches are able to perform the task just as well without preparatory inputs, i.e., with external inputs forcefully confined to the movement epoch – an illustratory example is shown in Figure 1B.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the authors' own modeling work shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Motor preparation is known to benefit behavior by shortening reaction times and enabling more accurate execution.
source: Motor preparation is known to benefit behavior (e.g. by shortening reaction times and enabling more accurate execution Riehle and Requin, 1989; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007; Michaels et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Motor preparation may facilitate motor learning.
source: and may facilitate motor learning (Sheahan et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2022)
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The high density of M1 neurons projecting directly to the spinal cord suggests that motor cortical outputs control lower-level effectors with little intermediate processing.
source: Specifically, the high density of M1 neurons projecting directly to the spinal cord (Dum and Strick, 1991) suggests that motor cortical outputs control lower-level effectors with little intermediate processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical observations cited from prior work.

claim: For preparatory processes to avoid triggering premature movement, any pre-movement activity in the motor and dorsal premotor cortices must engage the pyramidal tract neurons in a way that ensures their activity patterns will not lead to any movement.
source: For preparatory processes to avoid triggering premature movement, any pre-movement activity in the motor and dorsal premotor (PMd) cortices must therefore engage the pyramidal tract neurons in a way that ensures their activity patterns will not lead to any movement.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the anatomical constraint mentioned previously.

claim: Preparatory activity can be constrained to evolve in a nullspace of the motor output.
source: While this can be achieved by constraining neural activity to evolve in a nullspace of the motor output (Kaufman et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Previous network models of delayed reaches typically assume that the cortical network receives preparatory inputs during a fixed time window preceding the go cue.
source: Such an explanation could not be obtained from previous network models of delayed reaches, as they typically assume from the get-go that the cortical network receives preparatory inputs during a fixed time window preceding the go cue (Sussillo et al., 2015; Kao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of prior modeling approaches, supported by citations.

claim: In previous models, pre-movement activity is by design a critical determinant of the subsequent behavior.
source: In this case, pre-movement activity is by designing a critical determinant of the subsequent behavior (Sussillo et al., 2015; Kao et al., 2021; Zimnik and Churchland, 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the modeling assumptions in prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The authors modeled the motor cortex as an input-driven dynamical system and used optimal control to find spatiotemporal patterns of network inputs that minimize a cost functional.
source: We considered the dynamics of an RNN model of M1 coupled to a model arm (Todorov and Li, 2003), and used a standard control cost functional to quantify and optimize performance in a delayed-reaching task. We used the iterative linear quadratic regulator algorithm (iLQR) algorithm (Li and Todorov, 2004) to find the spatiotemporal patterns of network inputs that minimize this cost functional, for any given network connectivity.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The authors considered an inhibition-stabilized network which was shown previously to capture prominent aspects of monkey M1 activity.
source: We considered an inhibition-stabilized network – which was shown previously to capture prominent aspects of monkey M1 activity (Hennequin et al., 2014; Kao et al., 2021)
evidence: This describes the choice of network model, justified by prior work cited.

claim: Optimal control of the inhibition-stabilized network model requires preparation, with optimal inputs arising well before movement begins.
source: and found that optimal control of the model requires preparation, with optimal inputs arising well before movement begins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by modeling results in Figures 2-3.

claim: Preparation can be largely explained by two quantities summarizing the dynamical response properties of the network.
source: We then generalized insights from those systems back to high-dimensional networks using tools from control theory, and found that preparation can be largely explained by two quantities summarizing the dynamical response properties of the network.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Optimal control of compound reaches leads to input-driven preparatory activity in a dedicated activity subspace prior to each movement.
source: Consistent with recent experimental findings (Zimnik and Churchland, 2021), we observed that optimal control of compound reaches leads to input-driven preparatory activity in a dedicated activity subspace prior to each movement.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by modeling results in Figure 6 and consistent with cited experimental work.

claim: The target had to be reached within 600 ms of a go cue that follows a delay period of varying (but known) duration.
source: The target had to be reached within 600 ms of a go cue that follows a delay period of varying (but known) duration.
evidence: This describes a task constraint in the model.

claim: Network activity began changing well before the go cue for any single optimally performed reach.
source: For any single optimally performed reach, we found that network activity began changing well before the go cue (Figure 2B, bottom)
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Network activity changes before the go cue were driven by inputs that arose early.
source: and that this was driven by inputs that arose early (Figure 2B, middle).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Preparatory network activity cancels in the readout such that the hand remains still.
source: Thus, although preparatory network activity cancels in the readout (such that the hand remains still; Figure 2B, top)
evidence: This is demonstrated in the modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The preparation index rose sharply as the delay period increased, and eventually plateaued at approximately 1.3 for delay periods longer than 300 ms.
source: We found that the preparation index rose sharply as we increased the delay period, and eventually plateaued at ∼1.3 for delay periods longer than 300 ms (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The decrease in target cost was due to the model producing faster reaches.
source: The former effect was due to the model producing faster reaches (Figure 2C inset; hand position for a reach with [red] and without [blue] preparation)
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling results shown in Figure 2C inset.

claim: The decrease in effort cost arose from smaller control inputs being necessary when preparation was allowed.
source: while the latter arose from smaller control inputs being necessary when preparation was allowed.
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling results.

claim: The presence of a delay period changes the optimal control strategy for reaching, and increases performance in the task.
source: Together, these results suggest that the presence of a delay period changes the optimal control strategy for reaching, and increases performance in the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results in Figure 2.

claim: Delaying the reach beyond approximately 300 ms brings little benefit, with all components of the cost stabilizing past that point.
source: The results above show that delaying the reach beyond ∼300 ms brings little benefit; in particular, all components of the cost stabilize past that point (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The optimal controller made very little use of any preparation time available up to 300 ms before the go cue.
source: We found that the optimal controller made very little use of any preparation time available up to 300 ms before the go cue
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: With longer preparation times, external input continued to arise just a couple of hundred milliseconds before movement initiation.
source: with longer preparation times, external input continued to arise just a couple of hundred milliseconds before movement initiation
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Single neuron firing rates remained remarkably similar irrespective of the delay period.
source: and single neuron firing rates remained remarkably similar (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PCA projections of the firing rates traced out similar trajectories irrespective of the delay period.
source: This was also seen in PCA projections of the firing rates, which traced out similar trajectories irrespective of the delay period (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Networks of E and I neurons embed two main motifs of effective connectivity: feedforward ('nonnormal') connectivity and anti-symmetric connectivity that causes oscillations.
source: Specifically, networks of E and I neurons have been shown to embed two main motifs of effective connectivity which are revealed by appropriate orthogonal changes of basis: (i) feedforward ('nonnormal') connectivity whereby a 'source mode' of E-I imbalance feeds into a 'sink mode' in which balance is restored, and (ii) anti-symmetric connectivity that causes the two populations to oscillate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about network dynamics.

claim: Optimal control of both nonnormal and oscillatory dynamical motifs generally led to preparatory dynamics, with inputs arising before the go cue.
source: We found that optimal control of both dynamical motifs generally led to preparatory dynamics, with inputs arising before the go cue (Figure 4B and E, bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: In the feedforward motif, the amount of preparatory inputs appeared to depend critically on the orientation of the readout.
source: In the feedforward motif, the amount of preparatory inputs appeared to depend critically on the orientation of the readout.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: When the readout was aligned with the sink mode, the controller prepared the network by moving its activity along the source mode.
source: When the readout was aligned with the sink (brown) mode (Figure 4B, left), the controller prepared the network by moving its activity along the source (orange) mode (Figure 4C, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: When the source mode was read out, the optimal strategy was to defer control to the movement epoch.
source: Thus, here the optimal strategy was to defer control to the movement epoch, during which the transient growth of network activity along the readout rested entirely on adequate control inputs.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Of the two extreme readout configurations in the nonnormal network, reading out the sink mode yielded a smaller overall optimal control cost.
source: Importantly, of the two extreme readout configurations discussed above, the first one yielded a smaller overall optimal control cost (by a factor of ∼1.5).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results.

claim: In the oscillatory network, the optimal control strategy yielded the same results irrespective of which unit was driving the hand's acceleration.
source: A key difference however was that the flow field was rotationally symmetric such that no distinction could be made between 'source' and 'sink' units – indeed the optimal control strategy yielded the same results (up to a rotation of the state space) irrespective of which of the two units was driving the hand's acceleration (compare left and right panels in Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The optimal controller consistently moved the network's activity along the output-null axis during preparation in the oscillatory network.
source: Nevertheless, the optimal controller consistently moved the network's activity along the output-null axis during preparation, in such a way as to engage the network's own rotational flow immediately after the go cue (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The optimal way to control the movement depends not only on the strength and flow of the internal network dynamics, but also on their interactions with the readout.
source: Crucially, we found that the optimal way to control the movement depends not only on the strength and flow of the internal network dynamics, but also on their interactions with the readout.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results in Figure 4.

claim: For a network to benefit from preparation, there must exist activity patterns that are momentarily output-null yet seed output-potent dynamics that subsequently move the arm.
source: First, there must exist activity patterns that are momentarily output-null (i.e. do not immediately cause movement) yet seed output-potent dynamics that subsequently move the arm.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the modeling results.

claim: The nullspace of the readout must be sufficiently 'observable' for a network to benefit from preparation.
source: In the language of control theory, this criterion implies that the nullspace of the readout must be sufficiently 'observable' – we captured this in a scalar quantity α (Methods; Kao and Hennequin, 2019; Skogestad, 2007).
evidence: This is a hypothesis formalized using control theory concepts.

claim: There must be a sizeable cost to performing the movement in an entirely input-driven manner without relying on preparation.
source: Second, there must be a sizeable cost to performing the movement in an entirely input-driven manner without relying on preparation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the modeling results.

claim: The readout must be of limited 'controllability' for a network to benefit from preparation.
source: In other words, the network should be hard to steer along the readout direction, i.e., the readout must be of limited 'controllability' – we captured this in another scalar quantity β (Methods).
evidence: This is a hypothesis formalized using control theory concepts.

claim: Zimnik and Churchland (2021) concluded that each reach in a sequence was successively seeded by its own preparatory activity.
source: This study concluded that, rather than the whole movement sequence unrolling from a single preparatory period, each reach was instead successively seeded by its own preparatory activity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from prior experimental work, supported by citation.

claim: Preparatory and movement activity patterns in the model were well segregated in their respective subspaces in the single-reach task.
source: We performed a similar analysis (Methods) and verified that preparatory and movement activity patterns in the model were also well segregated in their respective subspaces in the single-reach task (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: For double reaches with a long pause, the preparatory subspace was transiently occupied twice, with the two peaks occurring just before the onset of each movement in the sequence.
source: For double reaches with a long (600 ms) pause, the preparatory subspace was transiently occupied twice, with the two peaks occurring just before the onset of each movement in the sequence (Figure 6B, bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The occupancy during the 'compound' reach started rising prior to the first movement before decaying very slightly and peaking again before the second reach, indicating two independent preparatory events.
source: Notably, the occupancy during the 'compound' reach (without pause; Figure 6C) also started rising prior to the first movement before decaying very slightly and peaking again before the second reach, indicating two independent preparatory events.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The behavior of two preparatory phases in compound reaches arises from the requirement that the hand stop briefly at the first target.
source: In our model, this behavior can be understood to arise from the requirement that the hand stop briefly at the first target.
evidence: This is an explanation proposed for the modeling results.

claim: To produce the second reach, the hand needs to accelerate again, which requires transient re-growth of activity in the network.
source: To produce the second reach, the hand needs to accelerate again, which requires transient re-growth of activity in the network.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the modeling results.

claim: Given that the network's dynamical repertoire exhibits limited timescales, re-growth of activity is most easily achieved by reinjecting inputs into the system.
source: Given that the network's dynamical repertoire exhibits limited timescales, this is most easily achieved by reinjecting inputs into the system.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the modeling results.

claim: The 'independent' preparation strategy observed in monkeys is consistent with the optimal control of a two-reach sequence.
source: In summary, our results suggest that the 'independent' preparation strategy observed in monkeys is consistent with the optimal control of a two-reach sequence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results in Figure 6.

claim: Preparatory neural activity patterns arise from optimal control of reaching movements at the level of motor cortical circuits.
source: Overall, our results show that preparatory neural activity patterns arise from optimal control of reaching movements at the level of motor cortical circuits, thus providing a possible explanation for a number of observed experimental findings.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the modeling results throughout.

claim: The animal protocols were approved by the Stanford University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: The animal protocols were approved by the Stanford University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the experimental procedures.

claim: Both monkeys were trained to perform a delayed-reaching task on a fronto-parallel screen.
source: Both monkeys were trained to perform a delayed-reaching task on a fronto-parallel screen.
evidence: This describes the experimental task used in the cited studies.

claim: Recordings were made in the PMd cortex and in the M1 using a pair of implanted 96-electrode arrays.
source: Recordings were made in the PMd cortex and in the M1 using a pair of implanted 96-electrode arrays.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the cited studies.

claim: The authors used the planar two-link arm model described in Li and Todorov, 2004.
source: To simulate reaching movements, we used the planar two-link arm model described in Li and Todorov, 2004.
evidence: This describes the arm model used in the study.

claim: The authors used the iterative linear quadratic regulator (iLQR) algorithm to find the locally optimal inputs that minimize the cost function.
source: Throughout this work, we used the iLQR algorithm (Li and Todorov, 2004) to find the locally optimal inputs that minimize our cost function.
evidence: This describes the optimization method used in the study.

claim: iLQR is a trajectory optimization algorithm that can handle nonlinear dynamics and non-quadratic costs.
source: iLQR is a trajectory optimization algorithm that can handle nonlinear dynamics and non-quadratic costs.
evidence: This describes the properties of the iLQR algorithm.

claim: iLQR works by linearizing the dynamics and performing a quadratic approximation of the cost at each iteration.
source: iLQR works in an iterative manner, by linearizing the dynamics and performing a quadratic approximation of the cost at each iteration, thus turning the control problem into a local linear quadratic problem whose unique solution is found using LQR (Kalman, 1960).
evidence: This describes how the iLQR algorithm works.

claim: Inhibition-stabilized networks were generated according to the procedure described in Hennequin et al., 2014.
source: Those were generated according to the procedure described in Hennequin et al., 2014, with minor adjustments.
evidence: This describes the method for generating the network models.

claim: The procedure for generating inhibition-stabilized networks yielded strongly connected but stable networks with a strong degree of nonnormality.
source: This yielded strongly connected but stable networks with a strong degree of nonnormality.
evidence: This describes the properties of the generated networks.
